title: “We Have No One”: How Trump’s Dismantling of the VA Left a Veterans Hospital in Crisis
author: Hokyoung Kim
content:
John Falchetto was a survivor. In Vietnam, his river gunboat came under
devastating rocket fire. He was the only one to make it out alive. But this
February, Falchetto, who had just turned 80, began to have piercing stomach
pains. He was in distress for days. Finally, Falchetto went to the VA hospital
in East Orange, New Jersey.

![An ambulance with flashing lights pulls up to a hospital with illuminated
sliding doors. Two attendants rush a gurney with a person through the doors.

](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260929_va-
decline_kim_a2.jpg?w=752)

A CT scan of Falchetto’s abdomen suggested his appendix had not only burst,
but that it was gangrenous. His gut was so filled with bacteria and pus that
tissue was dying. Doctors wrote that he needed surgery immediately.

But that night, the hospital’s operating room was closed. Months earlier, the
ventilation system had malfunctioned, and the repair team was short-staffed.
So Falchetto lay there, his life in the balance, for seven hours.

This was not normal. But nothing had been normal at East Orange since
President Donald Trump returned to office last year and set his sights on the
VA.

The behemoth agency, which traces its roots to the Civil War, is both the
country’s largest healthcare system and one of its most effective. It provides
9 million veterans what is essentially socialized medicine, often for free,
under the cover of the American flag. The doctors, nurses and other staff are
employed by the government.

Despite [the occasional
scandal](https://www.cnn.com/2014/04/23/health/veterans-dying-health-care-
delays) and [persistent short-staffing](https://www.legion.org/information-
center/news/newsletters/2024/august/severe-shortages-of-doctors-and-nurses-
have-persisted-for-a-decade-at-va-facilities-report-finds), studies have shown
that the VA — where the doctors coordinate with one another and have deep
expertise on veterans’ needs — has[
better](https://www.heinz.cmu.edu/media/2022/February/veterans-taken-to-va-
hospitals-had-better-survival-rates-than-veterans-taken-to-private-hospitals)[
outcomes](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2812416)
than private care.

But in his second term, Trump has moved aggressively to upend this system,
embracing a [decades-long conservative
campaig](https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-administration-plots-costly-
private-care-expansion-for-veterans)n to effectively kneecap the VA’s
government-run healthcare and shift veterans toward private doctors and
hospitals.

Under Trump, the VA has increasingly acted like an insurer, paying doctors in
the community for vets’ care. This, the reasoning went, would allow the
government to cut thousands of needless bureaucrats while giving veterans more
choices if the VA can’t provide the care.

* * *

### Do You Have Information About the VA That We Should Know?

We’re still reporting. If you know more about this topic, please contact our
reporting team.

**Eric Umansky**

I’m looking for tips on the VA’s care of veterans, and I’m particularly
interested in hearing from healthcare providers and others who work at VA
hospitals. Contact me with tips by email or securely on Signal. I take
confidentiality seriously.

[Contact Me](https://www.propublica.org/people/eric-umansky)

* * *

“We love our veterans,” Trump said during an Oval Office photo op shortly
after his inauguration. “We are going to take good care of them.”

Days after that pronouncement, [a memo
leaked](https://www.afge.org/globalassets/documents/generalreports/2025/va-
memo-3-4-25.pdf) showing the administration was considering sweeping job cuts
at the agency. “Things need to change,” warned Doug Collins, Trump’s new VA
secretary, in a video message to staff.

After pushback from vets groups and others, the administration retreated from
its threat of mass layoffs. But it found another, less attention-getting way
to shrink the VA.

If Trump’s appointees couldn’t lay off employees, they would make work
conditions so untenable that staffers would leave on their own.

The administration [canceled the contracts of the agency’s unions — citing
national security concerns](https://www.fedmanager.com/news/va-terminates-
most-union-contracts). They ordered remote staffers back to the office. Elon
Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency [demanded employees
report](https://www.npr.org/2025/02/23/nx-s1-5306366/musk-federal-worker-
email-confusion) what they had accomplished each week. And the administration
offered staffers early retirement packages and other incentives [to
quit](https://federalnewsnetwork.com/veterans-affairs/2025/05/few-va-health-
care-employees-qualify-for-resignation-incentives-some-are-leaving-anyway/).

Throughout it all, the VA’s leadership said front-line medical workers would
be immune from any cuts. But amid the upheaval, many left anyway.

Six months after Trump entered the White House, the VA had 3,800 fewer
doctors, nurses and other “mission critical” staff than it did at the start of
his term, according to [the department’s own
data](https://department.va.gov/employees/va-workforce-dashboard/). While the
losses made up a small percentage of overall employees, the drop compounded
longstanding shortages — and contrasted sharply with a hiring spree under
President Joe Biden that had begun to address them. Many of the front-line
workers who quit in Trump’s early days have never been replaced. Instead, [the
VA has eliminated](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/03/us/politics/veterans-
affairs-nurses-doctors-cut.html) thousands of open positions, including
doctors, nurses and other providers.

The administration has denied that it is hurting veterans’ care. “There’s
actually an excitement about what’s going on,” said Collins, a former personal
lawyer for Trump, in congressional testimony this spring. A spokesperson said
the eliminated jobs for healthcare providers were simply “not needed.”

That is not what we have found. Over months of reporting, ProPublica has
watched the East Orange VA Medical Center — a typical agency facility — spiral
downward. The hospital and its affiliated facilities in New Jersey lost nearly
a tenth of the staff they had when Trump took office.

Over the past two years, a VA watchdog report shows, the number of roles with
“[severe
shortages](https://www.vaoig.gov/sites/default/files/reports/2026-09/vaoig-26-01046-271_-_final.pdf)”
in East Orange has tripled, from around 30 to roughly 90. Among them:
oncologists, radiologists, surgeons, cardiologists, anesthesiologists,
critical care doctors, nurses, mechanics, cleaners — nearly every job that
makes a hospital run.

“It’s scary,” one East Orange administrator said in a meeting this year. “We
have no one.”

It’s not just there. According to the VA’s watchdog, nearly all VA hospitals —
97% — reported having severe shortages of doctors. (The agency argues that the
report — titled in part, “Staffing Shortages” — is simply about shortages of
candidates and not actual staffing.)

The exodus of healthcare providers has increasingly forced veterans into the
private care program — called Community Care — that the Trump administration
has pushed. Amid soaring caseloads there and what a government report
describes as [“insufficient
staffing,”](https://www.vaoig.gov/sites/default/files/reports/2026-09/vaoig-25-03946-211.pdf)
many vets have been facing interminable waits.

ProPublica and other outlets have previously detailed problems with particular
areas of VA care under Trump, [such as mental
health](https://www.propublica.org/article/veterans-affairs-hospital-
shortages-trump). But our reporting suggests far more care for veterans is
being put at risk.  

At East Orange, the damage wrought by the administration’s approach has cut
like a scythe across nearly every area of the hospital.

Wound care is harder to get, since the nurses who specialize in it have mostly
gone. The standard tests for blood clots weren’t available for most of the
year, because there were no technicians. Even radiation treatment was stopped
for months, after one of the key specialists left.

“Care has gotten worse for the patients,” said one doctor. “The services
available. The wait times. We’re not providing the care that we wish we
could.”

Another doctor, who recently quit, recalled how vets coming in with chest
pains couldn’t get cardiac tests for months. “It felt dangerous practicing in
a place like that,” said the physician, who, like others, declined to be named
for fear of retribution. “That’s something you don’t want on your conscience.”

VA employees across the country told ProPublica they are seeing remarkably
similar issues at their hospitals.

In Albuquerque, New Mexico, short-staffing forced the hospital to take many of
its beds offline and stopped [it from operating on severe heart
attacks](https://www.vaoig.gov/sites/default/files/reports/2026-08/26-00043-232_-_final.pdf).
Surgeries — on lungs and spines — have also been suspended for months at the
VA hospital near St. Petersburg, Florida. At both hospitals, government
reports found, Trump’s touted private care program was also overwhelmed and
understaffed, further fueling delays in care.

> “Care has gotten worse for the patients. The services available. The wait
> times. We’re not providing the care that we wish we could.”
>
> East Orange VA doctor

Surgeries and other critical care have also been delayed at the Minneapolis
VA. A staffer there shared a friendly looking notice tacked to a bulletin
board in May: “No SOD coverage” — meaning, no surgeon on duty — “until further
notice.” Radiation treatment was also suspended there because one of the
machine’s operators quit. A Minneapolis doctor recalled that meant having to
put a vet with cancer-riddled bones on a rattling ambulance ride every day,
rather than simply wheel him down the hall. The doctor said each bump on the
winter roads caused the vet excruciating pain: “It was miserable.”

A longtime oncologist who works with VA hospitals around the country told me,
“Care is collapsing from the inside.”

Starting in July, ProPublica repeatedly asked the VA about evidence we’d found
that short-staffing is hurting veterans’ care. We asked to interview Collins
and the leadership of East Orange. The VA did not make them available. Nor did
it address the specifics ProPublica shared on care.  

In a general statement, the VA said care has improved under Trump. “This
Administration is solely focused on measuring VA’s success by how well it
serves Veterans,” said agency spokesperson Quinn Slaven. He cited a record
number of appointments for both direct and private care over roughly the past
year. Slaven also noted that the private care program began under the first
Trump administration and was also embraced by the Biden administration.

As for East Orange, Slaven said the facility is outperforming private
hospitals on certain metrics, such as diabetes care and some cancer
screenings. Slaven also said more appointments were completed in fiscal year
2025 — which ran from October 2024 through September last year — than in any
year of the Biden administration.

Citing privacy law, the VA noted it could not address individual cases without
a waiver from the patient or appropriate family member. While ProPublica spoke
with veterans’ family members and loved ones, none chose to sign.  

We did, however, also ask the VA about the general issues surrounding those
cases — such as East Orange’s OR being closed — and the agency did not
respond.

In speaking to us, family members expressed surprise about their loved ones’
care. Falchetto’s brother, Tony, knew his brother had appendicitis, but hadn’t
known that the OR in East Orange was closed. “Oh my god,” Tony exclaimed when
I told him that his brother didn’t get timely care.

This story is based on internal documents, emails, agency data, recordings and
interviews with more than two dozen current and former VA staffers, along with
veterans and their families.

Contrary to the administration’s rhetoric, what emerges is a portrait of an
institution in trauma.

![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20260929_va-
decline_kim_a4-v2.jpg?w=752)

### “It Felt Like Bullying”

As soon as Trump was reelected, healthcare providers and other staffers at
East Orange could feel the barometric pressure plummeting and the storm
arriving.

The incoming administration’s plans for federal employees had long been clear.
“We want to put them in trauma,” said Russell Vought in 2023, before he became
Trump’s chief of the Office of Management and Budget. “We want them to not
want to go to work.”

Just days into the new administration, officials imposed a rigid return-to-
office policy, even as many staffers — from schedulers to radiologists reading
digital scans — had shifted to remote work in recent years. An internal agency
watchdog later wrote that the edict caused a “[system
shock](https://www.vaoig.gov/sites/default/files/reports/2026-09/vaoig-25-00242-195_final.pdf)”
at East Orange, whose outdated infrastructure and long-mothballed rooms
couldn’t handle the influx.

“I love working with vets, and I’ve never wanted to work anywhere else,” said
one medical provider at East Orange who rattled off a list of edicts. “You’re
this little person, and the full weight of the federal government was on you.
It felt like bullying. It was very, very stressful.”

That May, Collins appeared before Congress and promised that the
administration would not cut care: “We’re going to maintain VA’s mission-
essential jobs, like doctors, nurses, claims processors, while phasing out
nonessential roles, like interior designers and other things — DEI.”

Two months later, [the agency touted](https://news.va.gov/press-room/va-to-
reduce-staff-by-nearly-30k-by-end-of-fy2025/) the loss of nearly 30,000
staffers. “VA is headed in the right direction,” Collins said in a statement
announcing the losses. It was hard to know if the remaining staff agreed,
[since officials
canceled](https://www.militarytimes.com/veterans/2025/08/21/va-cancels-plans-
for-employee-satisfaction-survey-this-year/) the VA’s employee satisfaction
survey.  

Among the most essential staff at VA hospitals have long been the specialty
doctors, with their years of extra training. Recognizing their importance —
and their potential to earn far more in the private sector — bipartisan
legislation, which Biden signed into law in January 2025, allowed the VA to
pay top-notch doctors more than the standard government rate.

But [under Trump, the department](https://www.govexec.com/pay-
benefits/2026/04/va-failure-use-new-authority-boost-pay-doctors-bipartisan-
criticism/412755/) didn’t use that authority for more than a year — even as
more and more specialty doctors were leaving.

So, amid the departmental tumult, East Orange’s doctors began to exit, and
they often weren’t replaced.

Six months into the administration, East Orange was down five psychologists,
two of its four general surgeons and 18 nurses, among others, according to
data obtained through a public records request.

The departures weren’t limited to front-line providers. So-called support
staff were leaving too. The effects could be just as devastating. In East
Orange, the medical physicist calibrated radiation machines. When he quit, the
hospital had to suspend radiation treatment for months.

That left a veteran named Dennis in the lurch. The 72-year-old Vietnam vet had
advanced colorectal cancer, which was causing rectal bleeding. Dennis’
bleeding — and his pain — could be reduced with radiation. It might also give
him more time. But suddenly, East Orange couldn’t provide the treatment.

In early August, Dennis’ case was transferred to the Community Care program,
which reroutes vets to private providers. Except East Orange’s Community Care
office had also been losing staff and was overwhelmed with requests. Weeks
passed as Dennis waited, even as his doctors messaged at least five times that
he needed to be seen, as one put it, “ASAP.”

![Aerial view of a person holding their head in their hands. They are sitting
in an office chair in front of computer screens and piles of
paper.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20260929_va-
decline_kim_b3-v2.jpg?w=752)

He finally got an appointment for a consultation — the first step toward
radiation — for Sept. 12. But Dennis never made it.

He died on Sept. 4.

### Winter Comes to East Orange

A half dozen oncologists and surgeons told me that delaying treatment by more
than a month and a half was problematic. At the least, they said, the delays
almost certainly made his last weeks more painful. One told me he gives
patients in Dennis’ condition radiation “within hours.” (ProPublica is
withholding the veteran’s last name at the request of his family, which wants
to maintain their privacy.)

Other veterans at East Orange faced the same dynamics: They were shunted to
private care after their VA doctors and others left — and then they got stuck
in the system since the office that handles private care — Community Care —
was so overloaded. “That volume just keeps going up,” one administrator said
at a meeting last November. The reason for the increased referrals to
Community Care? She explained: “We just do not have the providers to provide
the care.”

That winter the short-staffing and its effects spread across East Orange.

Staff were told via email that because of “urgent nurse staffing levels,”
eight of the hospital’s roughly 60 general admission beds were being “taken
out of service.”

“That was a big chunk of our beds,” said one of East Orange’s doctors. “I
don’t recall ever having to close that many.” Without beds, the doctor
explained, veterans often “stay in the emergency room, which is not ideal.”
Indeed, [studies have shown](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41672875/) that
leaving patients in the ER is dangerous and results in higher mortality rates.  

A vet at one of East Orange’s campuses wrote to Trump complaining about short-
staffing. He soon received a response signed by the president. “Every American
owes our veterans an eternal debt of gratitude,” Trump said in the one-page
letter, “and under my leadership, they will always have the loyalty, respect,
and support they have earned and so dearly deserve.”

> “You’re this little person, and the full weight of the federal government
> was on you. It felt like bullying. It was very, very stressful.”
>
> VA healthcare provider

Around the same time, the hospital also had to shutter its operating room.

In December, part of the operating room’s air flow system had malfunctioned,
contaminating the surgical instruments. Breakdowns like this weren’t unusual.
East Orange was built 70 years ago, and its infrastructure showed it. But now
the hospital mechanics who kept it all running were quitting. In interviews,
they cited the same downward spiral that healthcare staffers did: As coworkers
left, the staff who remained had to pick up the load, further increasing the
strain of their jobs.

This put even more strain on a department that was already “severely
understaffed” before Trump, said Irvin Webb, who worked as an air systems
technician before he left the VA in May 2025. As a result of the departures,
he said, repairs ended up taking longer. (Air conditioning equipment mechanic
and air conditioning equipment operator were both among the many East Orange
positions categorized as having severe shortages in this year’s VA survey.)

Medical staff felt the impact. One doctor calculated that the OR has been down
nine times over the past year — compared with once the year before.

After the air flow malfunction in December, the**** OR was out of action for
roughly three weeks. It then reopened for planned surgeries but remained
closed for emergency and off-hours surgery for more than another month.

Then, on Feb. 12, Falchetto came to East Orange with a burst, gangrenous
appendix.

He arrived in the early evening. Doctors noted that he had abdominal pain,
vomiting and diarrhea, and described the results of Falchetto’s CT scan as
“worrisome.” The doctors wrote that Falchetto needed surgery, but, as one
physician noted, there was a “lack of OR capability.” And so, despite his life
depending on quick intervention, Falchetto had to leave the hospital that was
treating him.  

At about midnight, East Orange arranged for Falchetto to be transferred to the
VA hospital in Manhattan. It’s less than an hour away. But Falchetto ran into
yet another problem: Instead of arranging an emergency transfer, the
administrators scheduled him to be moved when the transport unit started its
morning shift around 7.

Falchetto was finally taken to the Manhattan VA the morning of Feb. 13. About
12 hours had passed since he had arrived at East Orange’s emergency room. The
Manhattan surgeons operated on him immediately, noting “perforated
appendicitis with gross fecal spillage.”

![An aerial view of two doctors working under operating room lights.

](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260929_va-
decline_kim_c2.jpg?w=752)

They also recognized something even more ominous: sepsis, a life-threatening
reaction to infection.

Falchetto never recovered. Doctors documented “worsening septic shock.” He had
a catastrophic heart attack a week later. With little brain activity,
Falchetto was transferred to hospice.

He died on March 7.

### “Imminent Risk to Patient Care”

It’s impossible to say for certain whether short-staffing caused Falchetto’s
death. He was severely ill when he arrived at East Orange and may have died
even if he got proper, timely treatment. But he didn’t get that.

“If I were the family, I’d sue everyone,” one of the doctors involved in
Falchetto’s case told ProPublica. “He should have been operated on
immediately.”  

By last spring, managers at East Orange were sending increasingly dire alarms
internally. One email in March — just a few days after Falchetto died — warned
that the shortages were preventing proper care.

The crises began coming in quick succession, one more desperate than the next.

Both of the hospital’s orthopedic surgeons left. And wound care became a
particular problem. The East Orange VA previously had three nurses who
specialized in the area. By this spring, just one remained, according to East
Orange staffers. She would have to commute dozens of miles between East
Orange’s hospital and its satellite clinics and nursing home.

“I’m not going to have time for anything,” the nurse told colleagues in a
meeting about the changes.

A few months later, a veteran arrived at East Orange with a diabetic ulcer —
essentially an open wound — on his left foot. His records state that the wound
“significantly increased in size” but that he hadn’t been seen by a wound care
specialist amid shortages.

> “If I were the family, I’d sue everyone.”
>
> East Orange VA doctor

It was the VA’s nearby nursing home — which the agency calls a community
living center — that raised the starkest alarm. A message to the staff on
April 10 warned of an “extreme shortage of CLC nursing staff with an imminent
risk to patient care.”

An administrator wrote in the message that the nursing home was taking
emergency action to cut the number of veterans allowed at the facility from
192 to 180. Soon the cap was reduced again, to 170.

What that meant is that vets who qualified for spots would be mostly turned
away.

Typically, the East Orange hospital could function as a kind of temporary
overflow facility for the nursing home. And the nursing home could do the same
for East Orange, taking some patients when the hospital was full.  

But now neither could handle any more. On May 20, a notice went out to staff
saying the hospital couldn’t accept patients from the nursing home that day.

What’s more, 17 veterans who needed admission were instead housed in the ER.
Other hospitals also sometimes do that, but at East Orange the problematic
practice went from rare to “far more common,” one doctor involved recalled.
They were stuck there at least a day. “They’re in bed all day,” said the
doctor. “It’s essentially a cot.”

![Rows of flags stand in a field with flat gravestones.
](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260929_va-
decline_kim_c4.jpg?w=752)

### “People Are Falling Through the Cracks”

The day after the ER pileup, Collins, the VA secretary, arrived on Capitol
Hill to testify again. He bristled when he was asked about how staff cuts and
eliminated positions were affecting care.

“[There is nothing they cannot
hire](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IoKQiRBbYWA),” Collins told the
lawmakers. If hospitals need a doctor, “they hire the doctor.”

Soon after, Collins [quietly imposed staffing
caps](https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2025/09/va-set-caps-its-workforce-
eliminate-positions-and-tighten-controls-hiring/407877/). What’s more, even
when hospitals do have the authority to hire, the pall hanging over the agency
now has impacted recruiting. As ProPublica reported last year, many doctors
have [turned down VA job offers](https://www.propublica.org/article/veterans-
affairs-hospital-shortages-trump) amid the ongoing turmoil. Nearly 4 in 10 of
the roughly 2,000 doctors offered jobs from January through March last year
rejected them. That is quadruple the rate of doctors rejecting offers during
the same time period in 2024.

At the time of Collins’ testimony, the VA had around 5,100 fewer doctors,
nurses and other “mission critical” staff than it did at the start of the
Trump administration, a 3.4% drop. Under Biden, by contrast, the VA had been
staffing up.

> “There is nothing they cannot hire.”
>
> Doug Collins, VA secretary

At East Orange, staffers told me the hospital had no vascular techs for most
of this year, meaning there was no one to run tests on arteries and veins. And
on the oncology ward, internal records show the team assigned to help patients
navigate their treatment was down to just one nurse.

The providers who have stayed have been overwhelmed by vets’ needs — a dynamic
that employees say is playing out in VA hospitals across the country. “People
are falling through the cracks, and now they’re not getting help,” said one
primary care physician at a VA clinic in Missouri.

“I’ve been working from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.,” she said. “I’ve had to take mental
health breaks because I’ve been so stressed. I’ve been near suicidal. It’s not
normal.”  

### Coins, Not Care

On a late August morning, a smattering of black SUVs and police cars pulled up
to a VA campus near East Orange. Collins and a gaggle of aides stepped out of
the caravan and went inside.

The VA secretary visited two departments. One was the chaplains’ unit, which,
like so many units within East Orange these days, is “severely understaffed,”
according to an internal presentation. (Collins is an ordained Baptist
minister and once served as a Navy chaplain.)

The other was the residential PTSD unit. Staffers had arranged for Collins to
meet with veterans, messages show. The event was not open to the media, but,
according to staff and a vet who were there that day, Collins sped through the
visit and did not stay long to speak with the vets.

On his way out, Collins stopped for a moment to talk to a veteran without legs
in a wheelchair. After Collins strolled away, I asked the veteran what they
discussed. “He just thanked me for my service and gave me one of these,” said
Willie Johnson, showing me a commemorative coin that says, “Secretary of
Veterans Affairs, Douglas A. Collins.”

I asked Johnson whether he had noticed changes in care since Trump returned to
office. “Oh yes,” he said, noting that even food has gotten worse (among the
positions with severe shortages at East Orange: food service worker).

The day after Collins’ visit, an email went out to staff. A “particularly
meaningful part” of the visit, the email from a top administrator said, was
the opportunity to recognize the service of five employees with Collins’ coin.

Among the recipients was the head of the maintenance department — the
diminished unit that’s struggled to keep the operating room open.  

Last week, as we were preparing to publish this story, a doctor at East Orange
told me of a development: a backup generator had failed, and the OR was closed
yet again.

The post [“We Have No One”: How Trump’s Dismantling of the VA Left a Veterans
Hospital in Crisis](https://www.propublica.org/article/east-orange-va-
hospital-veterans-decline-new-jersey) appeared first on
[ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
